entries.title: Iran closes language center in Tehran, France vows response
entries.summary: In response to the Iranian authorities' decision to close a French language center affiliated with its embassy in Tehran, France vowed to take appropriate measures.
entries.content:
Iran

Iran closes language center in Tehran, France vows response

September 21, 2026

In response to the Iranian authorities' decision to close a French language center affiliated with its embassy in Tehran, France vowed to take appropriate measures.

Paris will summon Iran's ambassador and take appropriate measures in response after Iranian authorities closed a French language center affiliated with its embassy in Tehran, the French Foreign Ministry said on Sunday.

"This new attack against France's cultural presence in Iran, following the assault on two staff members of the French embassy last July, is unjustifiable and ​unacceptable," the ministry's spokesperson Pascal Confavreux said in a statement.

What do we know about the center's closure?

Earlier on Sunday, Iranian authorities announced the closure of a French language center in Tehran following a judicial order from the prosecutor's office.

"The illegal center affiliated with the French embassy in Tehran, which has operated for years under the guise of language instruction, was closed," the judiciary's Mizan news website said, referring to the French Language Center (CLF).

The Iranian judiciary accused the center of conducting "illegal acts that violated diplomatic conventions".

It also accused the center of having "abused its status as a language training facility" and of having sought to "identify and build networks among the country's elite figures while facilitating their departure."

Tensions between Paris and Tehran

France has previously dismissed such allegations. The country claims that there has been a pattern of intimidation in recent months as it has sought to increase support for and contact with Iran's civil society following the crackdown on protests at the beginning of this year.

Tensions between Tehran and Paris have been escalating in recent years. Last month, France expelled two Iranian diplomats in response to the brief detention and prohibition of two French envoys to the Islamic Republic. Tehran accused the diplomats of interfering in its internal affairs.

Diplomats said Iran was also upset by a recent social media post from French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot commemorating the fourth anniversary of Mahsa Amini's death, which sparked protests nationwide.

In response, on Friday, Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi called the post "crocodile tears" and accused Paris of slaughtering 1.5 million Algerians during Algeria's war of independence.

The two ministers are scheduled to meet on Tuesday at the United Nations' annual gathering of world leaders.

Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah

entries.title: Canada, France agree to closer ties in defense, economy
entries.summary: Amid strained relations with the US, French President Emmanuel Macron and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announced closer economic and defense ties.
entries.content:
Canada

Canada, France agree to closer ties in defense, economy

September 20, 2026

Amid strained relations with the US, French President Emmanuel Macron and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announced closer economic and defense ties.

French President Emmanuel Macron and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announced deeper cooperation between their countries in many areas, including defense, energy, and business.

The two leaders made the announcement on Sunday from Saint Pierre and Miquelon, a small French territory just off the Atlantic coast of Canada.

According to a statement from Carney's office, the leaders discussed aerospace, energy, critical minerals, and advanced technologies, such as quantum computing, satellites, and supercomputing.

This move is another step in Canada's accelerating turn toward Europe, as both countries are experiencing strained relations with the US.

The meeting between Macron and Carney follows up on Carney's visit to Brussels, during which the EU offered Canada "associate member" status.

What did the leaders say?

"We both believe that our countries are two great, independent nations who want to remain so," Macron said at the joint news conference, adding that France and Canada would work together for closer ties on fishing, security and energy.

"We both believe in democracy, the rule of law, respect for free and fair trade, the science on which our decisions are based, and the strategic autonomy that we defend," Macron said. "And this is what very deeply unites Canada and France, Canada and the European Union."

Meanwhile, Carney said: "The time has come to tighten our links between Canada and France, between Canada and the European Union — links based on the values we share."

"History remembers those who... defend their sovereignty, those who stay true to their values," Carney stressed in his speech.

However, he also proposed that France, Canada, the United States and China work together on artificial intelligence.

Where is Saint Pierre and Miquelon?

Saint Pierre and Miquelon, a French overseas territory, is located off the coast of Newfoundland and has a population of fewer than 6,000 people.

It is France's only remaining possession in North America and a remnant of its former vast territories in what are now Canada and the United States. One of Canada's provinces, Quebec, has French as its sole official language.

Macron's three-day visit to Saint Pierre and Miquelon is the first by a French president in over a decade. Carney is the first Canadian prime minister to visit the territory.

The leaders' meeting comes at a time of strained relations with the US. Ottawa has strongly rejected President Donald Trump's repeated remarks about making Canada the 51st US state.

Last Monday, Trump posted a map of North America on social media. The map depicted Canada, Greenland, Mexico, much of Central America and the Caribbean, and Iceland in the colors of the US flag.

Several French overseas territories were also included in the image, such as Guadeloupe, Martinique, and Saint Pierre and Miquelon.

However, upon his arrival in the territory late Saturday, Macron reaffirmed its status as French territory and dismissed "strange ideas" on the subject.

Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah

entries.title: German state elections deal a blow to Chancellor Friedrich Merz
entries.summary: Elections in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania have dealt the CDU a historic defeat while the AfD saw a massive gain. The pressure on Germany's unpopular chancellor is mounting.
entries.content:
Germany

German elections deal a blow to Chancellor Friedrich Merz

September 20, 2026

Elections in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania have dealt the CDU a historic defeat while the AfD saw a massive gain. The pressure on Germany's unpopular chancellor is mounting.

Two of Germany's 16 federal states, Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, have just elected new state legislatures. The results for Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU) represent yet another major blow in turbulent times both nationally and internationally.

In northeastern Germany, projections suggest that the CDU narrowly failed to clear the 5% threshold for representation in parliament, a historic first in the party's history.

In the German capital, the party that led the state government, lost nearly a third of its support, dropping to around 20%.

Just minutes after the first projections were released, Merz made a statement: "We can't sugarcoat the results in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania — it was a disaster." As for the heavy losses in Berlin, he described the outcome there as "reasonable."

For the CDU, this marks the third electoral defeat in two weeks. In the state election in Saxony-Anhalt on September 6, the party came in far behind the Alternative for Germany (AfD), which the Office for the Protection of the Constitution has classified as partially far-right extremist.

In the wake of this debacle, Merz, whose term began in 2025, appeared visibly shaken.

At the federal level, Merz governs in coalition with the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), which saw mixed results in Sunday's state elections.

With around 36% of the vote, SPD state premier Manuela Schwesig — who has been in office since 2017 — finished just behind the far-right AfD in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. The AfD, on the other hand, nearly doubled its share of the vote compared to state elections in 2021, coming in first at 38%.

In Berlin, however, the SPD's share of the vote fell by a third to 12%, while the AfD became the third-largest party, winning 16% of the vote.

Meanwhile, the new frontrunner in the German capital is the socialist Left Party, with about 25%. It too was able to double its share of the vote, just as the AfD did in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. With the support of the SPD and the environmentalist Greens, the socialists — whom the CDU has labeled radical leftists and antisemites — would be able to form a coalition.

Berlin set to get a left-wing mayor

If this happens, Elif Eralp would be the first person from the Left Party to serve as mayor of Berlin. Leading up to the election, Eralp, the daughter of Turkish exiles, shared her vision in an interview with DW: "My vision for Berlin is an affordable Berlin where everyone — regardless of their background, religion, language or income — can lead a good life in dignity," Eralp said.

In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, a coalition of SPD, the Left Party and the Greens is the most likely outcome. State Premier Schwesig said she was committed to a "stable democratic government."

Meanwhile, AfD co-leader Alice Weidel once again declared on election night that the CDU's containment strategy of refusing to cooperate with her party had failed. Speaking on the public television network ZDF, she said: "Our long-term goal, of course, is to hold coalition talks with the CDU."

The AfD and the Left Party are stronger than the CDU and SPD

Both election results reflect widespread dissatisfaction among the population with Chancellor Merz and the coalition he leads with the SPD. In nationwide opinion polls, the governing coalition no longer has a majority. Here, too, the AfD is clearly in the lead, while the SPD is only narrowly ahead of the Left Party.

Parties on the political fringes are now gaining significantly more support at both the federal and state levels than the ruling parties, which are frequently embroiled in arguments on the federal level. These disputes often arise in connection with the reform agenda announced months ago by Chancellor Merz, aimed at bringing the rapidly rising costs of health, long-term care and pension insurance under control.

Despite yet another election setback, the German chancellor intends to stay the course: "The reforms must go ahead. Of course, this puts us all in a difficult situation. But we will shoulder this responsibility. I will shoulder this responsibility," he said.

After lengthy discussions, the coalition had already reached an agreement on health care reforms. Many things, like drugs and dental prosthetics, will become more expensive, while family insurance coverage will also be scaled back. These are all measures that won't win any new support for the already unpopular government. The same goes for the ongoing debate over reforms to the pension system, which is set to be supplemented by increased private retirement savings.

'I want to move our country forward'

Merz acknowledged that these changes would bring burdens and new uncertainties for many people. Nevertheless, he remained confident: "I want to move our country forward. I am also firmly convinced that the success of our reforms will not only improve our society but also boost our self-image and our image in the world."

In foreign policy as well, Merz — and with him the federal government — is coming under increasing pressure as a result of the election results in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. The AfD, which is particularly strong in eastern Germany, opposes military support for Ukraine in its fight against Russia's invasion.

'What needs to be done now requires backbone, resolve and patience'

This complex situation makes things even more difficult for the federal government — and Merz is well aware of this. Taking stock of the heavy election defeats suffered by his CDU, he said: "What needs to be done now requires backbone, resolve and patience. I will muster that — as chairman of the CDU and, above all, as the chancellor of our country."

This article has been translated from German.

entries.title: AfD makes gains in state elections, but has no government options
entries.summary: Despite making significant gains in both Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the far-right AfD remains without options to form a state government.
entries.content:
Germany

AfD makes gains in elections, but has no government option

September 20, 2026

Despite making significant gains in both Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the far-right AfD remains without options to form a state government.

The Alternative for Germany (AfD) made significant gains in the elections in northeastern Germany and in the capital, Berlin, but is likely to remain in the opposition in both states.

The Alternative for Germany (AfD) scored another election victory on Sunday evening, becoming the strongest party in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania with 37.9% of the vote, according to an exit poll by the polling firm infratest-dimap on election night.

That put the far-right party just ahead of the Social Democrats (SPD), whose dramatic comeback in the last few weeks, led by incumbent State Premier Manuela Schwesig, fell just short, with 35.7% of the vote on Sunday evening. The final results may vary as votes are counted.

The AfD was not short of confidence. Even before the first exit poll results were announced, AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla told public TV network ARD, "We clearly have a mandate to govern here," before adding that the party would offer coalition talks to all the other parties.

Chrupalla also said he expected Chancellor Friedrich Merz to resign now. "That would truly be a relief for this country," he said.

The AfD also made gains in the Berlin House of Representatives — the state parliament of the German capital — but fell far short of its own expectations on election night. According to infratest-dimap, it took 16.2% of the vote, though it had been polling at 18% only last week.

AfD: 'We are the new people's party!'

With Merz's center-right Christian Democrats (CDU) suffering heavy losses in both state elections, AfD party co-leader Alice Weidel said she now sees her party as the successor to the CDU.

"We are the new people's party in Germany," Weidel pronounced to public broadcaster ZDF, before criticizing the Christian Democrats for refusing to entertain the possibility of entering into a coalition with AfD: "We are holding talks because we haven't erected any firewalls." But Weidel did not explain what the policy talks with other parties would look like.

After the AfD's triumph in the state of Saxony-Anhalt on September 6, it has become clear that the party — some of whose members are considered a threat to Germany's constitutional order by German domestic intelligence agencies — is struggling to find political allies.

In that election, the AfD narrowly missed securing an absolute majority of seats in the state parliament and thus cannot elect the state premier on its own. In the struggle to form a governing majority, no party currently appears willing to enter into a coalition with the AfD.

No majorities for the AfD

However, the AfD's leading candidate in Saxony-Anhalt, Ulrich Siegmund, had made it clear that he would only lead a "stable" AfD government, ruling out a minority government tolerated by representatives from other parties. During the election campaign, he had gone even further, repeatedly stating that he would only serve as state premier in a single-party AfD government.

Since then, it has been unclear exactly what the AfD is aiming for. The AfD's national leadership appears to have a strong interest in seeing form any kind of government. This was underscored by Weidel, who said after the elections in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania that the AfD could take power "even in a minority government."

Weidel herself is said to have ambitions to succeed Merz as chancellor. She was already her party's chancellor candidate in the last federal election in 2025, and many top AfD officials also see her as the chancellor candidate next time round. A successfully formed AfD state government could potentially give those ambitions a boost.

However, the party's rise has also been accompanied by growing protests. In the elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin, it was evident that many voters mobilized to keep the AfD's votes in check.

AfD scandals during the campaign

The party also made several negative headlines during the election campaigns: In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, one AfD candidate had to pull out of the race when it emerged that he was a convicted bank robber. Another candidate withdrew his candidacy for the state parliament when it was revealed he had a DUI conviction and could no longer hold a driver's license.

In Berlin, meanwhile, drugs and Nazi memorabilia were found in the possession of a staff member of the party's lead candidate.

In the past, AfD politicians have repeatedly drawn criticism for making positive allusions to the Nazi era. One AfD European Parliament member posed with his hand on his heart in front of Adolf Hitler's "Führer Bunker" in Berlin, while one Bundestag member described himself as the "friendly face of National Socialism."

The influential AfD state leader in Thuringia, Björn Höcke, was twice fined for using a slogan of the notorious Sturmabteilung (SA), the paramilitary organization of Adolf Hitler's NSDAP party.

This article was translated from German.

entries.title: Germany faces energy tax losses as EV sales rise
entries.summary: The rapid shift to electric vehicles in Germany is cutting fuel tax revenue for the government. As EV sales surge, policymakers face growing pressure to find new ways to fund roads and transportation infrastructure.
entries.content:
September 20, 2026

The rapid shift to electric vehicles in Germany is cutting fuel tax revenue for the government. As EV sales surge, policymakers face growing pressure to find new ways to fund roads and transportation infrastructure.

"People are moving away from gasoline and diesel," Jens Boysen-Hogrefe, a tax and transportation expert at the Kiel Institute for the World Economy (IfW), told DW bluntly. "The boom in electric cars triggered by high fuel prices is accelerating the transition in drive technologies that was already planned anyway."

According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), sales of electric vehicles in Europe rose by nearly 30% in the first quarter of 2025 compared with the same period last year.

Norway is leading the way, with electric cars accounting for as many as 95% of all newly registered cars in the country.

The agency's "Global EV Outlook 2026" reveals that EV growth rates in Asia-Pacific countries, excluding China, were even more remarkable, with sales in some regions rising by up to 80%. In Latin America, that figure was about 75%.

Fossil fuels remain a tax windfall

The boom in electric mobility has not been met with universal enthusiasm in the German government, as charging an electric car does not incur energy taxes, but only minimal electricity taxes.

Currently, a liter of diesel in Germany is taxed at 47.04 euro-cents  (54 US cents per gallon), and a liter of gasoline at 65.45 euro-cents. On top of that, there is a carbon levy and a 19% value-added tax.

With gasoline priced at €2.10 per liter, taxes account for €1.14 of the total, meaning that more than half of the pump price goes to the government, according to the ADAC motoring club.

The current fossil-fuel-based system, with its energy taxes, truck tolls and CO2 tax, is very lucrative for the government, Boysen-Hogrefe said. "The finance minister doesn't benefit much when people drive electric cars," he noted. "Quite the opposite."

Energy tax revenue in decline

"If the shift to electric cars takes place and nothing changes in the tax system, the road system will become a money-losing venture for the federal government," Boysen-Hogrefe said, predicting billions of euros in losses.

According to Germany's Federal Statistical Office, revenue from the energy tax on diesel and gasoline fell from €37 billion in 2016 to €33 billion last year.

In 2022, a report by the scientific advisory committee to the German Transport Ministry projected that revenue from the energy tax would drop to as low as €5 billion by 2050.

Pressure to reform road funding

"The transition to electric vehicles has fiscal implications that have hardly been discussed so far," the report stated. The expected tax shortfalls add to the costly subsidies for electric vehicles that are currently still necessary to drive the transition forward, the report added.

In Germany, government incentives to purchase electric cars — amounting to several thousand euros per vehicle — were scrapped at the end of 2023.

Electric cars are still exempt from vehicle tax through 2035. And companies that invest in electric cars continue to enjoy tax benefits.

In their report, the transportation experts advised the government not to wait until the tax deficit becomes so large that it is forced to act.

That's because "the lead time for such measures spans several legislative terms," they argued.

Boysen-Hogrefe said fiscal pressure could now increase. If people continue to buy electric cars in droves, "the government can't just shrug it off," he said.

How other countries are responding

Countries such as the United Kingdom and Norway have already come up with measures to deal with the new situation.

In the UK, a levy on electric cars is set to take effect in April 2028. The so-called "Electric Vehicle Excise Duty" charges 3 pence (3.5 euro-cents) per mile (1.6 kilometers) on fully electric cars and 1.5 pence on plug-in hybrids.

Since 2024, New Zealand and Iceland have required annual odometer checks for electric vehicles to calculate mileage-based fees.

In Switzerland, meanwhile, electric vehicle owners will be required to pay a road-use charge from 2030, either through a weight-based fee per kilometer or a tax on electricity purchased at charging stations.

Meanwhile, Norway, a trailblazer for electric vehicles, has restricted the VAT exemption for electric cars starting this year. It has also introduced a weight-based purchase or registration tax and tolls.

Are road tolls the answer?

In Germany, many experts are advocating for a passenger car toll to compensate for the shortfall in energy tax revenue while also taking road use more fully into account.

"The recommended policy option is a distance- and traffic-based toll," according to a recently published  study by the University of Münster.

"If we realistically assume that policymakers will shy away from this step, the vignette solution is recommended," according to the report.

Under a vignette system, drivers pay a flat fee for road use over a defined period.

"If this, too, encounters insurmountable political resistance, the only solution left is to raise the motor vehicle tax," they concluded.

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: Peter Thiel: Power, Palantir, and the antichrist
entries.summary: He was early to back Facebook, early to back Donald Trump, and is one of the world’s richest people. But from his theories on the antichrist and AI to his distinctive politics, Peter Thiel is hard to pin down.
entries.content:
Argentina

Peter Thiel: Power, Palantir, and the antichrist

September 20, 2026

He was early to back Facebook, early to back Donald Trump, and is one of the world’s richest people. But from his theories on the antichrist and AI to his distinctive politics, Peter Thiel is hard to pin down.

He may not hog the limelight in the same way as Donald Trump, Elon Musk, or many of his other friends and associates, but Peter Thiel has a fair claim to be one of the world's most influential figures — as well as one of its richest.

Born in 1967 in Frankfurt am Main in what was then West Germany, the Thiel family moved to the US when Peter was just a year old. The family also spent six years in South-African occupied Namibia from 1971 to 1977.

Thiel's later rise to prominence came on the back of his tech firms and investments. His first major success was Paypal, a digital payments provider with which Musk was initially involved. Thiel then became the first outside investor in Facebook.

Today he also owns part of Musk's SpaceX, as well as OpenAI, and multiple other companies. Forbes puts his personal wealth at $35.7 billion (€31.1 billion).

But perhaps his most noteworthy company is Palantir. The surveillance, AI, and data-analytics company has won government contracts worth billions to create software for the Pentagon as well as US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). The company released a 22-point manifesto in April that critics said bore the imprint of "techno-fascism."

But Thiel could be considered as influential in politics as he is in business, and not just in the US.

Though several European countries, including the UK, the Netherlands, France, Germany, and Spain are starting to reevaluate or end their governmental and military links with Palantir due to security concerns, the company is deeply embedded in security systems across the globe.

Thiel himself has recently moved to Argentina, where he has reportedly held talks with the country's right-wing president, Javier Milei, as the government proposes a series of regulations that include incentives for foreign companies and targets investments in AI data centers. 

Early Trump support paid off

Thiel was an early backer, and later advisor, of Donald Trump, donating $1.25 million to Trump's 2016 election campaign and speaking at the Republican National Convention in the same year, at a time when Silicon Valley was broadly considered to be Democrat-leaning. Bar a hiatus between 2023 and 2025, he has been a generous donor to Republican campaigns and figures, including Vice President JD Vance.

Thiel's own political beliefs are not easy to pin down. He's been described as a libertarian nationalist and consistently expressed the belief that "technology is the alternative to politics."

He also shows a distrust of authorities, regulation, and liberal elites. This is partly born of a frustration with what Thiel considers inefficient decision-making by elected officials and voters.

"It's bordering on fascism," Max Chafkin, who wrote a 2021 biography of Thiel, told Time magazine. "He talks about how companies are better run than governments because they have a single decision-maker — a dictator, basically. He is hostile to the idea of democracy. That's pretty scary when you consider the role the companies that he's been involved in play."

These beliefs seemed to start to rise to the surface during his time at Stanford University in California. Thiel railed against the prevailing liberal campus ideology and founded the Stanford Review, a publication to express those contrary beliefs, something that would echo his current disdain for beliefs labeled as "woke."

Christianity, the antichrist, and AI

Thiel was raised in a strongly Christian household, and there is little doubt that his religion has colored his life and career. Thiel recently described himself as a "small 'o' orthodox Christian," something which seems to influence his conservative politics. His homosexuality, and marriage to American financier Matt Danzeisen, seem to many go against that grain. But paradox is not unusual for Thiel.

More recently, he has become preoccupied with the concept of the antichrist, touring with a series of lectures all over the world during the last few years. Rather than the figure depicted in the Bible, Thiel sees this as someone, or some group, who will deliver the apocalypse "by playing on our fears of technology and seducing us into decadence with the antichrist's slogan: Peace and safety."

Among those who have been, somewhat vaguely, cast in the role of soldiers of the antichrist have been environmental activist Greta Thunberg, whom he sees as a "Luddite who wants to stop all science," or governments that seek to regulate AI. He accused Pope Leo XIV of "working for the Chinese communists" in July after the pontiff warned about the "risk of dehumanization" by AI.

Despite his deep association with tech, Thiel also benefits from his relationships with powerful people, Musk, Trump, and Vance among them.

"I've built some great friendships over the years with people I've worked with," Thiel told the Washington Post in 2014. "And I think that's a really important part of what enables one to be successful in the long run in our society."

Using Vance to future-proof his interests?

Many observers think that Thiel may be using his relationship with Vance to help protect himself and his business interests in the future, with the vice presidentconsidered the most likely Republican to succeed Trump.

The pair met back in 2011 when Thiel gave a talk at Yale Law School. Vance, whose religious beliefs and politics have since shifted, wrote in Christian magazine The Lamp that Thiel "defied the social template I had constructed — that dumb people were Christians and smart ones atheists."

Thiel then reportedly became a mentor figure for Vance, before smoothing the relationship between Vance and Trump as Vance U-turned from previous opposition to the president to join his 2024 ticket. Most notably though, Thiel donated $15 million to Vance's Senate campaign in 2022, the largest amount ever donated to a single US Senate candidate.

The recent calls to slow the pace of AI, made in part by CEOs in similar positions to Thiel, may end up having an impact on Thiel's business interests. But his distinct character and connections have so far kept him a step ahead.

Edited by Carla Bleiker

entries.title: Russia: Ukrainian drone strike on Moscow kills 2
entries.summary: An oil refinery was hit in one of the largest attacks so far on the Russian capital, as the country holds a parliamentary election. Meanwhile, at least four people were killed in Russian strikes in Ukraine's Kyiv region.
entries.content:
Russian Federation

Russia: Ukrainian drone strike on Moscow kills 2

September 20, 2026

An oil refinery was hit in one of the largest attacks so far on the Russian capital, as the country holds a parliamentary election. Meanwhile, at least four people were killed in Russian strikes in Ukraine's Kyiv region.

Two people were killed in a Ukrainian drone attack on the Moscow region, local authorities said Sunday, with an oil refinery in the region also being hit.

Energy infrastructure has been repeatedly targeted by both Ukraine and Russia, despite US President Donald Trump saying both sides had agreed to stop.

Ukraine's repeated targeting of oil refineries has led to oil product shortages and fuel price increases in Russia.

Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the strike had "a very significant impact," saying the oil in the hit refinery funds "billions of dollars to sustain the war machine."

"Moscow must end its brutal war and choose peace instead of building layered rings of air defense at the expense of other regions," Zelenskyy posted on X.

According to Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin, more than 1,600 drones have been intercepted by Russia since Saturday, including 450 aimed at the Russian capital, making it one the largest Ukrainian drone attacks on the city since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.

Moscow mayor accuses Ukraine of trying to disrupt parliamentary election

Sobyanin said that numerous drones had made it to the oil refinery, and another one hit an apartment. The scale of the damage done to the refinery has not been confirmed.

This comes as Russia is entering the last day of its three-day parliamentary election.

Sobyanin said the "unprecedented attack was clearly planned with the aim of disrupting the elections."

Meanwhile, in the eastern Ukrainian, Russian-occupied region of Kherson, a drone attack on a bus had killed two people, including an election official, Russian state news agency RIA reported.

Three children killed in Kyiv region

In Ukraine, four people were killed in a Russian drone attack in the Kyiv region, local authorities said.

Among the casualties are a mother and her two 3-year-old children, as well as a girl who was taken to hospital in another district and later died.

The southwestern Fastiv district suffered damage to homes and industrial buildings.

Russia's Defense Ministry said a warehouse of drone and missile maker Fire Point was struck in the Kyiv region. It also hit a cargo vessel and a postal logistics center in the Odesa region, saying both were used for military shipments.

Russia has been repeatedly carrying out drone attacks on the Ukrainian capital in recent weeks.

Edited by: Karl Sexton

entries.title: Ed Sheeran speaks on Gaza in concert after Macklemore controversy
entries.summary: Sheeran called the Hamas-led attack in Israel "horrific" and described the war in Gaza as "catastrophic and unjustifiable" during his first concert since the Macklemore controversy erupted.
entries.content:
United States of America

Ed Sheeran speaks on Gaza after Macklemore controversy

September 20, 2026

Sheeran called the Hamas-led attack in Israel "horrific" and described the war in Gaza as "catastrophic and unjustifiable" during his first concert since the Macklemore controversy erupted.

British pop star Ed Sheeran has addressed the Israel-Palestine conflict, following a row over Macklemore's removal as a supporting act on the tour after the US rapper made pro-Palestinian comments on stage.

Performing in Philadelphia on Saturday night, the first concert since the controversy erupted, Sheeran said the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack, which killed around 1,200 people and saw dozens taken hostage, was "horrific."

He also described Israel's subsequent war in Gaza, which killed more than 70,000 people, as "catastrophic and unjustifiable and disproportionate."

Sheeran also condemned the "systemic injustice" in the occupied West Bank, where the Israeli government is pushing to expand Jewish settlements, which the United Nations has called a "flagrant violation of international law."

"I don't want to disappoint fans, and I've never wanted to be an activist musician, but this has put me in the middle of an important and passionate argument about freedom of speech and the most complex political issue on the planet," Sheeran said.

"I've had to take and make difficult decisions, and I am making mistakes, and I'm so, so sorry," he said.

Sheeran's latest statement was a reversal from his earlier stance on Instagram, when he said that his concert audiences "do not expect a political forum."

How did the controversy occur?

The pop singer's tour faced controversy after rapper Macklemore was dropped as a supporting act after he said "Free Palestine" at the opening of Sheeran's US Loop Tour in New Jersey in early September.

Sheeran has denied being responsible, saying venues had threatened to cancel shows if Macklemore remained on the tour.

Macklemore posted on Instagram that billionaire Robert Kraft had told Sheeran that the rapper would not be allowed to perform at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts, which he owns.

Several supporting acts subsequently withdrew in solidarity with Macklemore, including musician Finneas, Danish band Lukas Graham and Irish singer Aaron Rowe, as well as Sheeran's backing band — leaving one of the best-selling musical artists of all time without an opening act.

Pro-Palestinian demonstrators protest outside concert venue

Dozens of pro-Palestinian protesters rallied peacefully outside Philadelphia's Lincoln Financial Field before Sheeran's concert, waving Palestinian flags and chanting "Free, free Palestine."

Among the demonstrators was 18-year-old Brandon Ateke, who accused Sheeran of "complicity" with Kraft and others in silencing Macklemore.

"I decided to not attend the concert and instead attend the protest to bring light to the genocide going on in Gaza today," Ateke told AFP news agency.

The Palestinian Campaign for the Academic and Cultural Boycott of Israel (PACBI), a pro-Palestinian group, has called for a boycott of Sheeran's world tour.

entries.title: In cosmopolitan Berlin, elections still closed to foreigners
entries.summary: A quarter of Berlin residents will have no say in the German capital's city-state election because they lack citizenship. That's the highest proportion of residents excluded from the election yet, and many are unhappy.
entries.content:
Germany

In cosmopolitan Berlin, elections still closed to foreigners

September 20, 2026

A quarter of Berlin residents will have no say in the German capital's city-state election because they lack citizenship. That's the highest proportion of residents excluded from the election yet, and many are unhappy.

Abdu, an Egyptian software developer, ended up in Germany's capital more or less by chance seven years ago. "I wouldn't say I chose Berlin," he told DW. "It was just that the company that offered me a job was here."

But now he loves it. The culture is "better than any other city I have experienced," he said. That's partly because of its diversity, but he also likes the way Berliners approach life. "They're more interested in living than just working," he said. "Here I feel life is more relaxed, and this also offers the opportunity for people to get more creative."

But there's plenty about the city that he's not particularly happy with, including Berlin's rapidly rising rental prices, and the notoriously opaque bureaucracy is a constant source of annoyance. "I myself would like to start my own business, but it is difficult because of all the bureaucracy," he said.

In general, Abdu is dissatisfied with Berlin's current government, a conservative-led coalition of the Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) — but the trouble is, as a non-German national, he has no say in deciding whether it should stay in office or not. That is particularly frustrating at the moment, when the streets are bristling with campaign posters ahead of the election on September 20.

"We are people who pay taxes, but we don't have any representation at all, even on local level," he said. "The cuts to health care and German courses, for example, affect me directly."

Berlin: Bigger and more international

The German capital is growing and becoming more international. While the voting population in the upcoming election will be bigger than ever — mainly because the voting age has been lowered to 16 — so is the number of the disenfranchised.

Of Berlin's population of 3.9 million, a full quarter — around 976,000 adults — cannot vote because they don't have German citizenship. That number has doubled since 2011.

This is partly because of Germany's political structure. In Germany and across Europe, citizens of other EU countries can vote in municipal elections. In London, people from Commonwealth countries can do the same as long as they have UK residency. Spain, meanwhile, also has reciprocal voting agreements with several non-EU countries — in South America and elsewhere — that allow their citizens to vote in municipal elections, including for the mayors of Madrid and Barcelona.

Berlin's Sunday election is not a municipal one. Since Berlin is one of Germany's 16 federal states, it is holding a state election, which means that voting rights are more restricted. Berlin's municipal elections, where EU citizens are allowed to vote, only decide who governs the city's individual districts, and their political influence is limited.

The disenfranchisement is particularly acute in central Berlin. For that reason, Stefanie Remlinger, Green Party mayor in the district of Mitte, has organized a "symbolic election" for the non-Germans in her area — some 135,000 adults out of a population of 365,000. The initiative invites foreigners to vote at 15 ballot stations over a two-week period in early September to "raise awareness for the issue of voting rights for all."

"Mitte is an extremely heterogeneous district with a very international population," Remlinger told DW via video call from her office. "We have people from 170 different countries living here, and a lot of them don't have the right to vote. It's important to us to signal to those people that we value their opinions, that we see them."

Germany's 'rightward shift'

Getting people to vote in a meaningless election is a tough sell. Remlinger said she expected only a few hundred people to take part, and, anyway, she thinks the political climate in Germany is not exactly immigrant-friendly at the moment. Even in cosmopolitan Berlin, the anti-immigrant Alternative for Germany (AfD) is currently polling in second place, with nearly 20%.

"We as the Greens would liberalize voting rights even more, but I don't see the general debate in Germany going that way," she said. "We're fighting a rightward shift and a lot of hostility to immigration, and I think the chances of changing something on that issue right now are very bad."

To illustrate the state of the current debate, Remlinger mentioned a recent panel discussion she was part of, where a politician from the neoliberal Free Democratic Party (FDP) — a party that calls itself socially liberal — said voting rights shouldn't be opened to foreigners because they might start their own parties and take over the government. "And that from someone from the FDP!" said Remlinger, exasperated.

Abdu is also aware of this anti-immigrant shift in German politics. In fact, he said, that was one of the reasons he was considering leaving Germany altogether. "All the parties are trending right-wing, so it's getting more hostile," he said.

Is expanding voting good for the economy?

From an economic perspective, it might be considered a shame if qualified people like Abdu decided to leave Germany. The country lacks workers. The government estimates that the country will be short of about 440,000 workers by 2029, and even the AfD leadership claims it has nothing against immigrants who contribute to the economy.

Though some German cities and local authorities do have an elected advisory board for non-German residents, offering immigrants a real vote is frequently seen as a step too far.

Remlinger herself thinks that the best path to enfranchisement is not to offer foreign nationals voting rights, but to make it easier for immigrants to become German citizens.

That happens to be another one of Abdu's complaints about Berlin: "I applied for citizenship two years ago, and I didn't get any response," he said.

Germany has recently tightened citizenship rules again. Last year, Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government reversed the three-year "fast-track" citizenship option introduced under his predecessor, Olaf Scholz. Still, the government did keep another of Scholz's reforms, which allows people to apply for citizenship after only five years of residency.

More and more Berliners are in fact becoming German: 2025 saw about 39,000 people naturalized in the capital, 17,000 more than in 2024.

That avenue is still closed for Abdu, but in the meantime, a little more political participation would go a long way. "If I could vote, I would reconsider leaving, to be honest, because then I could affect things, but now I'm just like a bank machine — they come to me and take half of my salary."

Edited by: Rina Goldenberg

entries.title: India news: PM Modi says developing nations unfairly blamed for emissions
entries.summary: PM Narendra Modi has told a climate conference that developed countries emit six times more CO2 than India. Meanwhile, an IIT Bombay professor has been accused of caste abuse. DW has more.
entries.content:
India

Modi says developing nations unfairly blamed for emissions

Published September 19, 2026last updated September 20, 2026

PM Narendra Modi has told a climate conference that developed countries emit six times more CO2 than India. Meanwhile, an IIT Bombay professor has been accused of caste abuse. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Indian Prime Minister Modi tells a climate conference in Delhi that developing nations are unfairly blamed for emissions
  • IIT Bombay professor booked over alleged caste abuse after a student killed himself
  • Scottish-Sikh activist Jagtar Singh Johal, who had been detained in India for almost nine years without being convicted, has been granted bail
  • India had to replace Asian Games opening ceremony male flagbearer over missing ceremonial ⁠kit

Skip next section Smriti Mandhana becomes leading run-scorer in women's T20I history

Smriti Mandhana becomes leading run-scorer in women's T20I history

India thrashed Bangladesh by 114 runs in the Asian Games women's cricket semi-final on Sunday, with opener Shafali Verma striking a maiden century and Smriti Mandhana becoming the all-time leading run-scorer in women's T20 internationals.

Verma finished unbeaten on 100 off 49 balls, reaching triple figures off the final delivery of India's innings. It marked the first century in the history of Asian Games women's cricket, Indian wire service ANI reported, making Verma just the third Indian woman to score a T20I hundred, joining Mandhana and captain Harmanpreet Kaur.

Verma called the milestone long overdue: "It took a lot of years but finally it came, so I'm happy."

Mandhana reached her own landmark earlier in the innings, surpassing New Zealand's Suzie Bates to become the leading run-scorer in women's T20I history during a knock of 37 off 19 balls.

The pair put on a 71-run opening partnership inside the powerplay, setting up India's total of 195-4 in 20 overs at Korogi Athletic Park in Nagoya.

Bangladesh could not keep up the pace, with India bowling them out for just 81 in 15.4 overs.

The result sends India into Tuesday's gold medal final against Sri Lanka. Pakistan will face Bangladesh in the bronze medal match, also on Tuesday.

 

Skip next section WATCH — How foraging could protect Mumbai’s green lung

WATCH — How foraging could protect Mumbai’s green lung

In Mumbai, urban foraging is helping residents get in touch with nature, and this kitchen, associated with a Gujarati community, has unexpected environmental benefits.

Watch the full video below:

Skip next section Allahabad High Court orders police to protect interfaith lesbian couple

Allahabad High Court orders police to protect interfaith lesbian couple

The Allahabad High Court has directed Uttar Pradesh Police to ensure protection for a Hindu-Muslim same-sex couple whose live-in relationship was being threatened by their family members, local media reported.

In an order dated September 14, Justice Gautam Chowdhary held that the two women are free to live together peacefully without interference from family or anyone else, after personally interacting with the couple and finding both to be adults who had chosen to live together voluntarily, "without pressure, fear or undue influence," according to Bar & Bench, a legal news outlet.

The court directed that if any obstacle arises to their relationship, the police must immediately provide security once they verify both women are of legal age and living together by choice.

The petitioners' counsel told the court the couple faced serious threats to their lives from family members and needed immediate police protection.

The state government opposed the plea, arguing that "there was no acceptance for same-sex relationships" and that such relationships "affect the natural and traditional framework of society," the Times of India reported.

The court rejected that position, holding that living in a relationship is a fundamental right for consenting adult citizens, and that the absence of legal marriage recognition does not entitle anyone to threaten a couple's dignity or physical safety.

The ruling is the latest in a line of similar Allahabad High Court orders protecting same-sex and interfaith couples in Uttar Pradesh, building on earlier decisions, which cited the Supreme Court's 2018 ruling decriminalizing homosexuality in India.

Skip next section IIT Bombay under fire over caste abuse allegations after student's death

IIT Bombay under fire over caste abuse allegations after student's death

Mumbai police have filed a case against an IIT Bombay professor after a 20-year-old second-year student, Sahil Wakode, was found dead in his hostel room late Thursday, following allegations from his family that he had faced months of caste-based harassment.

Police registered charges against Suryanarayan D. and unidentified others under India's abetment-to-suicide law and provisions of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, local media reported.

Wakode's father, Ravindra Wakode, alleged in his complaint that his son had been subjected to sustained casteist remarks and mental harassment over roughly three months, and that the professor — who was invigilating an exam Wakode was attending on the day he died — used caste-based slurs against him.

The complaint also mentioned the institute's director. Similar complaints were shared by other students, according to The Wire. These allegations have not been independently established.

Meanwhile, IIT Bombay claimed Wakode was found using a mobile phone during the exam, but no disciplinary action was taken. Instead, he had been counseled and assured it would not affect his academic record before he returned to his hostel room.

Students at the scene allege that the professor was seen yelling at Wakode.

IIT Bombay said in a statement shared by local media that "the circumstances surrounding the death are being looked into by the appropriate authorities."

The case has drawn campus protests, with students at IIT Bombay demanding the resignation of both the director and the professor involved. It is reportedly the third student death by suicide at the institute this year, following earlier incidents in February and July.

Skip next section Developing nations unfairly blamed for emissions, Modi tells climate conference

Developing nations unfairly blamed for emissions, Modi tells climate conference

Prime Minister Narendra Modi has said developing countries are unfairly held responsible for carbon emissions despite their comparatively low per-capita output.

Modi made the remarks on Saturday as he inaugurated a two-day international conference on environmental and climate governance in New Delhi, organized by India's National Green Tribunal.

Speaking at the opening of the "Future of Environment and Climate Dynamics" conference at Vigyan Bhawan, Modi said, "We know that often the responsibility for carbon emissions is wrongly placed upon developing countries... the historical truth is that India's contribution per capita carbon emission is less than half of the global average."

"In developed countries, per capita carbon emissions are six times higher than in India."

He said India has consistently raised this point at global forums, including at the 2015 Paris climate summit, adding that India is the only G20 nation to have met its Paris commitments ahead of schedule.

The remarks come weeks after devastating floods hit India's northern neighbor, Nepal, killing over 1400 people. Nepal contributes roughly 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions, making it what the World Bank calls a "negligible contributor to climate change."

The conference, which ends Sunday, brings together judges and environmental officials from 17 countries as well as Indian Supreme Court and High Court judges, senior bureaucrats, and representatives of state environmental authorities, according to the Prime Minister's Office.

Skip next section WATCH — Basmati rice: India, Pakistan and the race for recognition

WATCH — Basmati rice: India, Pakistan and the race for recognition

One of the world's most valuable rice varieties, basmati carries strong historic ties to the Punjab region, which spans both India and Pakistan.

Both claim the premium, aromatic rice as part of their agriculture and cultural heritage, and are seeking European Union recognition for its geographical origin.

But years after the first application was filed in 2018, the fight over basmati rice is far from over.

Watch for more:

Skip next section ABVP sweeps DUSU polls as student safety, identity dominate campaign

ABVP sweeps DUSU polls as student safety, identity dominate campaign

The Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad (ABVP), affiliated with the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and its ideological parent Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), won three of four central posts in this year's Delhi University Students' Union elections, with its candidate Yash Dabas coming in from behind to be elected president.

Independent candidate Deepanshu Shokeen made history by winning the vice-presidential seat, defeating candidates fielded by both ABVP and the National Students' Union of India (NSUI), the student wing of the Indian National Congress.

In a university facing an acute shortage of hostels, student housing and safety dominated this year's campaign. This came after the September 6 collapse of a paying-guest building in Satya Niketan, near Delhi University's South Campus, which killed seven students. 

High rents, non-functional hostels, and a lack of affordable lodging near campus were central issues in candidate platforms.

Declaring his win, Dabas stressed the issue as he addressed the media: "We all witnessed the accident that occurred in Satya Niketan; we do not want such an incident to happen to anyone in the future, and that will be our first priority — conducting safety audits for every college, hostel, and PG."

Shokeen, an NSUI rebel who ran independently, built his campaign partly around the tragedy, vowing not to wear footwear until affected students got justice.

The election also unfolded in the shadow of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), a youth-led satirical protest movement that organized weeks of demonstrations at Delhi's Jantar Mantar earlier this year, demanding the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan over alleged irregularities in national entrance exams. 

While the CJP was not involved in the DUSU race directly, the movement shaped how many voters approached the election.

"Students were talking about what or ganisations stand for, whether they agree with their politics and whether voting can give them a greater say in issues concerning students," one student told news agency PTI, adding that many felt they "should not simply vote because a particular organisation has always been influential on campus."

Skip next section More uncertainty for Indian workers as Trump extends $100,000 H-1B visa fee

More uncertainty for Indian workers as Trump extends $100,000 H-1B visa fee

US President Donald Trump has extended the $100,000 fee on H-1B visa petitions through September 2027, the White House has said — a move that will be strongly felt in India, the largest source of H-1B recipients.

The extension, announced on Friday, keeps a policy first introduced in September 2025 in place. It excludes visa renewals and student visa holders transitioning to H-1B status. 

Trump also signed a proclamation directing tighter scrutiny of applications, instructing agencies to weigh employers' recent layoffs of American workers when reviewing petitions. 

The policy remains under legal challenge, with an appeals court reviewing a June ruling that found the fee unlawful.

The stakes are high for India: USCIS data for fiscal year 2025 showed Indian nationals accounted for 69.9% of approved H-1B petitions, far ahead of China's 12.1%.

When the fee first launched last year, it caused panic among Indian travelers, including passengers who deboarded a Delhi-bound flight fearing they'd be barred from returning.

Opposition Congress party leader Pawan Khera criticized the extension on social media, warning it would make it "harder for Indian students to enter the US workforce" and could drive a "talent drain" toward the UK, Canada and Australia.

He also targeted Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his perceived camaraderie with Trump, adding: "Modi bent over backwards to appease Trump. Trump got the appeasement. India took the humiliation and the hit."

Skip next section Surendra Koli, acquitted in Nithari serial killings case, found dead in suspected suicide

Surendra Koli, acquitted in Nithari serial killings case, found dead in suspected suicide

Surendra Koli, a key figure in India's notorious 2006 Nithari serial killings case who was acquitted of all charges last year, was found dead at a tea stall he operated in Haridwar.

Police are treating the case as a suspected suicide.

Residents discovered Koli's body inside the rented stall and alerted authorities, Haridwar City Deputy Superintendent of Police Shishupal Singh Negi told local media.

No suicide note was found and the body was sent for post-mortem examination as investigators look into the circumstances.

Koli first drew national attention in 2006, when he was a domestic worker at businessman Moninder Singh Pandher's home in Noida. The discovery of human remains, including children's, in a drain behind Pandher's house sparked a major investigation and nationwide outrage.

Koli was convicted and sentenced to death in multiple cases beginning in 2009. In October 2023, the Allahabad High Court acquitted both Koli and Pandher for lack of evidence.

Two key observations were made: Koli's confession was inadmissible, as it was extracted after a long, unauthorized interrogation in police custody without adequate legal safeguards, and the prosecution could not prove that the remains uncovered from the "open, public" drain were based solely on Koli's statements.

The decision was upheld by India's Supreme Court in late 2025.

Reports suggest he moved to the northern city of Haridwar after the acquittal. Police identified Koli through an Aadhaar card found on his body.

Skip next section India swaps flagbearer for Asian Games opening ceremony after kit mix-up

India swaps flagbearer for Asian Games opening ceremony after kit mix-up

A last-minute logistics problem has cost shot-putter Tajinderpal Singh Toor his spot as India's male flagbearer at Saturday's Asian Games opening ceremony in Nagoya, Japan.

Kabaddi player Pawan Sehrawat is set to step in instead, joining shooter Manu Bhaker, a two-time Paris Olympics bronze medalist, who will be India's female flagbearer.

Toor, who is chasing a third consecutive Asian Games gold in shot put, said he only learned of his selection as flagbearer a day earlier and that his kit was still back in India.

"I'm told that my kit will reach at 3 p.m. at the airport. Reaching the opening ceremony venue after collecting my kit from the airport on time will be very difficult," he told news agency PTI, adding that he had informed the Indian Olympic Association (IOA) that he would not be attending the ceremony.

The Indian Olympic Association said in a statement that Toor would be unable to serve as flagbearer "due to a technical issue."

The mix-up was one of several hiccups in the run-up to the Games, which open on Saturday with more than 17,000 athletes competing across more than 40 sports through October 4.

Organizers, working without a traditional athletes' village, have housed competitors in container-style huts, hotels and a cruise ship. There have been complaints over accommodation quality, transport delays, and a mistaken playing of North Korea's national anthem for South Korea's men's hockey team.

A tropical storm bearing down on the region threatens to cause further disruption as competition gets underway.

Skip next section Delhi High Court grants bail to Jagtar Singh Johal after nearly nine years in custody

Delhi High Court grants bail to Jagtar Singh Johal after nearly nine years in custody

The Delhi High Court granted bail to British national Jagtar Singh Johal in seven murder and terrorism-related cases, clearing the way for his conditional release after nearly nine years in Indian custody.

The court overturned a 2024 ruling that had denied him bail.

Johal, 39, a Sikh rights campaigner from Dumbarton, Scotland, was arrested in Punjab in 2017 shortly after he arrived in India for his wedding.

He was accused by India's National Investigation Agency of financing and courier work for the banned Khalistan Liberation Force in connection with a series of targeted killings in Ludhiana and Jalandhar districts between 2016 and 2017.

He was acquitted in a related case last year by a court in Moga, Punjab, while the Delhi cases had continued.

Johal has consistently denied wrongdoing and says he was tortured into signing a false confession. A United Nations working group ruled in May 2022 that his detention was arbitrary.

"Eight and a half years of arbitrary detention without a clear path to trial is not justice, it is unlawful suffering," UN human rights experts said in a statement earlier this year. "The prolonged uncertainty alone is a form of psychological torture."

Indian authorities have repeatedly rejected the torture allegations and insisted that due process was followed.

What did the court say in its ruling?

In its ruling, the court cited Johal's prolonged incarceration and the slow pace of the trial as grounds for bail, despite the strict conditions typically imposed under India's anti-terror law, the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act.

The court noted that 123 witnesses were yet to be examined and that proceedings were "certainly not likely to conclude any time soon."

The court imposed strict bail conditions, including surrendering his passport, restrictions on communication and social media activity, and regular reporting to the Investigating Officer. The court did not rule on the merits of the underlying case, leaving prosecutors free to have his bail revoked if the conditions of his release are breached.

Johal's brother, Gurpreet Singh Johal, who has campaigned for years for his release and urged successive UK governments to take action, called the ruling "a huge relief," the BBC reported.

"I had a long, sleepless night knowing that the decision would be made this morning. Now, all I can think about is Jagtar walking out of prison."

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Hello! This is Seerat from DW's Studio Delhi, bringing you the big news from and about India this weekend.

We lead our coverage with the news that British Sikh activist Jagtar Singh Johal, who had been detained in India for almost nine years without conviction, has been granted bail.

A UN panel in 2022 recognized it as a case of arbitrary detention, putting the Indian government's human rights record under the microscope.

The Asian Games kick off in Japan on Saturday, but it's not all smooth sailing for the Indian delegation's preparations.

India has announced a last-minute change of its male flagbearer for the opening ceremony after star shotputter Tajinderpal Singh Toor's ceremonial kit reportedly went missing.

Finally, counting is underway in elections for the Delhi University Student Union, this time under the shadow of the Cockroach Janata Party protests and the collapse of a building in the student hub of Satya Niketan.

For the latest on these stories and more, follow our blog.
